This vignette walks through a typical analysis: preparing texts, counting
features, checking what was counted and comparing results with the English
and French packages. The examples use the annotated sample documents shipped
with the package, so they run without downloading a parser model.

## From texts to features

`biber()` works on parsed text. A typical pipeline reads the texts, normalizes
typographic quotes, builds a corpus and parses it with udpipe or spaCy:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(readtext)
library(quanteda)
library(udpipe)
library(pseudobibeR.es)

docs <- readtext("corpus/*.txt", encoding = "UTF-8")
docs$text <- utf8::utf8_normalize(docs$text, map_quote = TRUE)
corp <- corpus(docs)

model <- udpipe_download_model(language = "spanish-gsd")
ud_model <- udpipe_load_model(model$file_model)
parsed <- udpipe_annotate(ud_model, x = as.character(corp), doc_id = docnames(corp))

features <- biber(parsed)
```

With spaCy, request morphology, which `biber()` needs:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
spacyr::spacy_initialize(model = "es_core_news_sm")
parsed <- spacyr::spacy_parse(corp, pos = TRUE, tag = TRUE, dependency = TRUE,
                              entity = FALSE, additional_attributes = "morph")
features <- biber(parsed)
spacyr::spacy_finalize()
```

## Reading the output

The sample documents are three short Spanish texts annotated with udpipe:

```{r}
library(pseudobibeR.es)
features <- biber(udpipe_samples, measure = "TTR", normalize = FALSE)
features[, c("doc_id", "f_01_past_tense", "f_17_agentless_passives",
             "f_18_agent_passives", "f_21_que_verb_comp")]
```

Each row is a document and each column a feature. With `normalize = FALSE`
the values are raw counts. The default, `normalize = TRUE`, gives rates per
1,000 words, which is what you want when documents differ in length. Words
exclude punctuation, symbols and numbers written in digits. Two columns are
measures rather than counts and are never normalized: f_43, the type/token
ratio, and f_44, the mean word length.

## Checking what was counted

`audit_features()` lists every occurrence behind a count, with its context.
Use it to check surprising values or to see what a feature captures:

```{r}
audit_features(udpipe_samples, feature = "f_18_agent_passives")
```

A whole category can be audited at once, with an optional sample:

```{r}
audit_features(udpipe_samples, category = "A", sample_n = 3, seed = 42)
```

## Features that differ from English

Most features carry over directly from English. A few are Spanish analogues of
English constructions. Their column names describe what is counted:

- `f_09_impersonal`: weather verbs and impersonal predicates (*Llueve*, *Es
  importante que…*), the counterpart of English *it*.
- `f_15_nominal_infinitives`: infinitives used as nouns (*Fumar perjudica la
  salud*, *el saber*), the counterpart of English gerunds.
- `f_60_reduced_complement`: an infinitive in place of a *que*-clause
  (*Creo haber entendido*), the counterpart of English *that*-deletion.
- `f_61_resumptive_relative`: a relative clause with a repeated pronoun (*el
  chico que hablé de él*), the colloquial alternative to *el chico del que
  hablé*.
- `f_28_gerund_reduced_relative` is always 0: a gerund modifying a noun (*una
  caja conteniendo libros*) is not standard Spanish.

The README lists every feature with examples, and `FEATURES_TECHNICAL.md` in
the package repository gives the exact rule behind each count.

## Comparing languages

Feature numbers are shared by the English (`pseudobibeR`), Spanish and French
(`pseudobibeR.fr`) packages: `f_15` is the same feature in all three. To get
the shared column names, for example to combine results across languages:

```{r}
shared <- biber(udpipe_samples, measure = "TTR", normalize = FALSE,
                feature_names = "shared")
names(shared)[c(10, 16, 19)]
```

`options(pseudobibeR.feature_names = "shared")` sets this for the whole
session. Even with shared names, a feature in two languages may be an analogue
rather than the identical construction, so compare scores across languages
with care, and do not score Spanish texts against English factor loadings
without validating them for Spanish.
